blueprint.title: PostgreSQL Connection Pool Quota Enforcement After Incident
blueprint.scenario: A DBA is investigating a production incident where a nightly analytics job exhausted all database connections, starving application traffic. The team runs a small in-house Python codebase (~1200 lines across 6 files) that includes a connection pool manager, a quota enforcer module, and a replay harness for post-incident analysis. After the incident, the DBA must run the replay harness against the recorded connection request log to reproduce the failure, then build a missing quota enforcement component that correctly gates connections per-role under the rules documented in the README, so the replay shows no role ever exceeding its limit.
blueprint.instruction_draft:
```
$ python replay.py --log incident.log
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "replay.py", line 14, in <module>
    from quota import QuotaEnforcer
ImportError: cannot import name 'QuotaEnforcer' from 'quota' (/app/quota.py)
```

The post-incident replay harness at `/app/replay.py` requires a `QuotaEnforcer` class in `/app/quota.py` that does not yet exist. The quota rules for each database role are documented in `/app/README.md`.

Build `QuotaEnforcer` in `/app/quota.py` so that `python replay.py --log /app/incident.log` completes without error and produces a report file at `/app/report.json`. The report must show the peak simultaneous connection count per role across the full log. The enforcer must correctly block any connection request that would cause a role's active connection count to exceed its configured limit at the moment the request arrives; blocked requests must be recorded in the report under `blocked_requests` per role.

After the replay completes, run `python verify_quota.py` — it must exit 0.
requirements: QuotaEnforcer class exists in /app/quota.py and is importable
/app/report.json contains peak_connections dict mapping each role to its observed peak simultaneous active connections
/app/report.json contains blocked_requests dict mapping each role to count of requests that were denied because the role was at its limit
python verify_quota.py exits 0 when run after replay
QuotaEnforcer enforces per-role connection limits as defined in /app/README.md at request-arrival time, not at request-completion time
QuotaEnforcer handles role aliases (one physical role may appear under multiple names in the log; the README documents the alias map) so aliases share the same quota pool
QuotaEnforcer correctly handles connections that never emit a disconnect event (they must be timed out per the idle_timeout_seconds value from config.yaml and released at that simulated time)
environment: FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm; apt-get: nothing extra; pip: pyyaml==6.0.2

/app/README.md: documents quota rules per role (app_writer: 10, app_reader: 20, analytics: 5, admin: 3), alias map (e.g., 'etl' is an alias for 'analytics', 'readonly' is alias for 'app_reader'), idle_timeout_seconds: 300, and the QuotaEnforcer interface (constructor takes config dict, methods: request(role, conn_id, timestamp) -> bool, release(conn_id, timestamp) -> None)
/app/config.yaml: machine-readable version of limits, aliases, and idle_timeout_seconds
/app/quota.py: exists but contains only a module docstring and a TODO comment — QuotaEnforcer class is missing

/app/pool.py: ~200-line connection pool implementation that calls quota.QuotaEnforcer; internally has working connect/disconnect logic; also contains a subtle bug: it flushes timed-out connections before checking the new request, but only for the requesting role, not all roles — this is plausible code, not the primary challenge
/app/replay.py: ~150-line harness that reads a log file of timestamped CONNECT/DISCONNECT events per role and conn_id, drives QuotaEnforcer calls in timestamp order, and writes report.json

/app/incident.log: ~3000-line log of real events from the incident night; the analytics role (and its alias 'etl') genuinely hit the limit; some connections never disconnect (they time out); the log contains interleaved events for all roles

/app/verify_quota.py: test harness that generates 50 synthetic log scenarios at verify time using a seeded RNG, runs replay.py on each, and checks report.json correctness against a reference computation embedded in the test; checks: peak_connections accuracy, blocked_requests accuracy, alias pooling, idle timeout release
/app/reference.py: internal reference implementation used only by verify_quota.py — it is not importable from quota.py path (lives in /app/tests/reference.py), so the solver cannot simply copy it
The alias map must be discovered from README.md or config.yaml — it is NOT mentioned in replay.py or pool.py
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two interact levers: (1) observe_not_read — the alias pooling bug and idle-timeout behavior only manifest when the harness runs on the real incident log or the synthetic logs; reading quota.py reveals nothing because the class doesn't exist yet; reading pool.py shows the flush-only-requesting-role logic but its effect on quota counts is only visible under concurrent load patterns in the log. (2) build_component — QuotaEnforcer must correctly implement: per-role limit enforcement at arrival time, alias resolution so 'etl' and 'analytics' draw from the same pool of 5 slots, and idle timeout expiry (connections with no DISCONNECT within idle_timeout_seconds are released at the moment a new request for the same pool arrives, which is when pool.py calls flush — the solver must mirror this exact timing or peak counts and blocked counts diverge from the reference). The verify_quota.py tests generate synthetic logs with adversarial alias interleaving and timeout edge cases not present in the visible incident.log.
blueprint.trap: A naive solver implements QuotaEnforcer with separate counters per role name string, making the replay pass on incident.log (which happens to have mostly 'analytics' events, few 'etl'), but the verify_quota.py synthetic scenarios flood through 'etl' alias first to fill the pool, then send 'analytics' requests that should be blocked — without alias pooling they go through. A second trap: the solver implements idle timeout by expiring connections at the wall-clock moment they cross the threshold, rather than at the moment pool.py requests a flush (i.e., when the next request for that role-pool arrives) — this changes which requests get blocked in tight-timing scenarios the synthetic logs include.
tests: Test 1 (import): verify_quota.py imports QuotaEnforcer from quota and instantiates it with the config dict — fails if class is missing or __init__ signature is wrong
Test 2 (basic limits): synthetic log with only 'app_reader' role, 25 simultaneous CONNECT events, no DISCONNECT; verify blocked_requests['app_reader'] == 5 and peak_connections['app_reader'] == 20

Test 3 (alias pooling): synthetic log alternates CONNECT events between 'analytics' and 'etl' to fill 5 slots, then sends more — verify both names draw from same pool and total blocked equals excess across both names

Test 4 (idle timeout timing): synthetic log sends 5 analytics CONNECTs, then waits (in log time) idle_timeout_seconds+1, then sends a 6th CONNECT without any DISCONNECTs — the 6th must succeed (timed-out slots freed) and blocked_requests['analytics'] must be 0

Test 5 (timeout triggers on arrival): synthetic log sends 5 analytics CONNECTs, advances time just under idle_timeout_seconds, sends 6th CONNECT — must be blocked; then advances 2 more seconds past timeout and sends 7th — must succeed; checks exact blocked count

Test 6 (incident log replay): runs replay on actual incident.log and checks that blocked_requests['analytics'] + blocked_requests['etl'] >= 50 (the real incident had many denied analytics connections), and peak_connections for app_writer <= 10

Test 7 (multi-role stress): 200-event synthetic log with all 4 roles and all aliases firing concurrently in timestamp order; reference computation independently calculates expected peak and blocked counts; asserts report.json matches within zero tolerance

verifier_knob.name: num_synthetic_scenarios
verifier_knob.effect: Lowering to 10 reduces alias-pooling and timeout edge case coverage, making partial implementations pass; raising to 200 with more adversarial alias-interleaving and sub-second timeout jitter makes even small timing errors fail

expected_failure_modes: Implements QuotaEnforcer with per-name counters instead of per-alias-pool counters; passes incident.log replay but fails alias-pooling synthetic tests

Implements idle timeout expiry eagerly (at the exact timeout timestamp) rather than lazily (at next request arrival for that pool), causing off-by-one blocked counts in tight-timing synthetic scenarios
Misses the alias map entirely (never reads README.md or config.yaml), so all alias-related tests fail

Builds a working QuotaEnforcer but does not handle the case where a conn_id is released twice (pool.py can call release on a conn_id that already timed out); double-release causes negative active count which makes subsequent blocks wrong

Correctly builds QuotaEnforcer but assumes CONNECT/DISCONNECT events are strictly paired and a conn_id is never reused; the incident log reuses conn_ids after timeout, causing the active-set tracking to over-count

speedrun: Write QuotaEnforcer to /app/quota.py: load config (limits, aliases, idle_timeout); build canonical-role map; per-pool active set (conn_id->timestamp); lazy timeout flush only when request arrives for that pool; request() resolves alias, flushes that pool's timed-out conns, checks limit, records or blocks; release() removes conn_id if present (guard double-release); track peak and blocked per canonical role; emit report.json
Debug alias pooling issue (if any) — re-read config.yaml alias map, fix canonical name resolution
Debug lazy timeout timing (if any) — re-read pool.py flush logic, fix to expire only at request arrival not eagerly
Debug conn_id reuse (if any) — add guard: if conn_id already in active set on CONNECT, treat as re-use (remove old, add new)
If still failing: cat /app/incident.log | head -50 to verify log format assumptions
invalid_failure_risks: The flush-only-for-requesting-role behavior in pool.py is discoverable by reading source, so the lazy-timeout trap is partially a read trap not purely a runtime trap — agents who read pool.py carefully will implement it correctly on the first try, reducing genuine difficulty

verify_quota.py generates synthetic scenarios at verify time using a seeded RNG — if the seed or RNG behavior differs between Python versions or platforms (e.g., 3.13 vs 3.12), test results could be flaky; the blueprint pins Python 3.13 but doesn't pin the RNG seed explicitly in the description, which could cause non-determinism

The instruction says reference.py is at /app/tests/reference.py and 'not importable from quota.py path' — but verify_quota.py presumably imports it; if verify_quota.py uses a relative import or the tests/ directory isn't on sys.path, it could fail for environmental reasons unrelated to the solver's solution

conn_id reuse behavior in incident.log ('the log reuses conn_ids after timeout') is listed as a failure mode but is not explicitly mentioned in the instruction to the solver — a solver might not discover this until verify_quota.py fails, and the error message may not clearly indicate the cause

The report.json schema (exact key names, structure for blocked_requests and peak_connections per role) needs to match what verify_quota.py expects exactly — if aliases are stored under canonical name vs. alias name, the check could fail ambiguously

The instruction doesn't specify whether peak_connections and blocked_requests in report.json use canonical role names or all alias names — this ambiguity could cause valid implementations to fail verification
review.reasons: The task is realistic, well-specified, and has a credible multi-trap structure (alias pooling, lazy timeout, conn_id reuse, double-release) that makes naive implementations fail on synthetic verification. The verifier uses fuzz-equivalence against a hidden reference, making it genuinely hard to pass with hollow solutions. The main concern is that all traps are discoverable by reading source files (pool.py reveals lazy timeout; config.yaml reveals aliases), which means a careful agent reading ~6 files could solve it in ~15 commands — pushing genuine_difficulty to 3 rather than 4-5, but still above threshold.
fixes: Make the lazy-timeout trigger less obvious in pool.py by commenting it as a 'performance optimization' rather than leaving the asymmetric flush logic self-evident — or move the timing behavior into replay.py so it's part of what the solver must infer from the log, not from reading pool.py
Explicitly document in the instruction what key names report.json should use for aliased roles (canonical name only, or all alias names) to prevent ambiguous failures
Add a note in the instruction that conn_ids may be reused after timeout, so this is a known requirement rather than a hidden trap that produces confusing error messages
Pin the RNG seed explicitly in the blueprint description and confirm it's hardcoded in verify_quota.py to prevent any risk of flaky synthetic test generation across environments
